stem: A 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan was purchased for m5.large in us-east-1. The team switches to m5.xlarge. How does the plan apply?

options.label: A
options.text: Exchange the plan for an m5.xlarge plan using the Savings Plans exchange feature.

options.label: B
options.text: The plan only covers m5.large; switching to m5.xlarge means paying On-Demand rates.

options.label: C
options.text: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply globally to any EC2 instance regardless of family or region.

options.label: D
options.text: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to all sizes within the committed family (m5) in the committed region (us-east-1), including m5.xlarge, up to the committed hourly spend.

distractors.B: EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover the entire instance family within the committed region, not just the specific size.
distractors.C: Compute Savings Plans are global; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are region-specific.
distractors.A: Savings Plans cannot be exchanged like Convertible RIs; they automatically apply to eligible usage.

explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans commit to a specific instance family in a specific region and cover all sizes (large, xlarge, 2xlarge, etc.) within that family. The committed hourly rate is consumed by whatever size is running in that family and region.

stem: EC2 instances generate many small S3 PUT requests (under 1 KB each) and S3 request costs are high. What architectural change reduces this?

options.label: A
options.text: Use SQS to queue objects and Lambda to batch them before a single S3 PUT.

options.label: B
options.text: Batch small objects into larger files before uploading; reducing PUT request count by combining objects significantly reduces S3 request costs per unit of data.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering; it reduces PUT request costs by optimizing storage operations.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch from S3 Standard to S3 Express One Zone for lower per-request pricing on high-frequency small-object workloads.

distractors.D: S3 Express One Zone has lower per-request costs but higher storage costs; batching is more universally effective.
distractors.A: SQS + Lambda batching adds latency and complexity; direct batching by the producer is simpler.
distractors.C: S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage class transitions; it does not reduce PUT request counts.

explanation: S3 charges per PUT request. Combining many small objects into fewer, larger uploads directly reduces the number of PUT API calls for the same data volume, lowering request costs.

stem: Reserved Instance and Savings Plan discounts in the management account should apply to all member accounts. What setting must be enabled?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable Cost and Usage Reports in the management account with consolidated billing; it automatically applies discounts across all accounts.

options.label: B
options.text: Transfer Reserved Instances to each member account using the RI Marketplace.

options.label: C
options.text: Create IAM policies granting each member account billing:ApplyDiscount permission.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable RI and Savings Plan sharing in the AWS Billing console; this allows discounts from the payer account to apply to member accounts' usage automatically.

distractors.C: There is no billing:ApplyDiscount permission; RI sharing is a billing-level setting.
distractors.B: RI Marketplace transfers RIs to individual accounts; this is the opposite of centralized sharing.
distractors.A: Cost and Usage Reports provide billing visibility; they do not control discount sharing.

explanation: Organizations consolidated billing aggregates usage. RI and Savings Plan sharing must be explicitly enabled in the Billing console for unused capacity and discounts to apply to member account usage automatically.

stem: An RDS instance has read IOPS consistently at maximum, causing query latency. Adding more provisioned IOPS is expensive. What is more cost-effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable automated backups with a smaller backup window to reduce I/O spikes, freeing IOPS for read queries.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable RDS Multi-AZ to distribute read traffic across primary and standby; Multi-AZ supports reads on the standby.

options.label: C
options.text: Add an ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of RDS to cache frequent read results; this reduces RDS read IOPS by serving cached responses for repeated queries.

options.label: D
options.text: Upgrade to a memory-optimized R-series instance; more memory allows RDS to buffer more data, reducing disk read IOPS.

distractors.B: Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads; it is for failover. Read Replicas serve reads.
distractors.D: A larger instance reduces read IOPS through buffer pool expansion but is typically more expensive than adding a caching layer.
distractors.A: Backup I/O occurs during the backup window; reducing it does not free steady-state read IOPS.

explanation: ElastiCache Redis serves repeated read results from memory, reducing the number of database queries hitting RDS. A 50-90% IOPS reduction is common for read-heavy workloads with temporal locality, making it more cost-effective than significantly increasing provisioned IOPS.

stem: Which AWS service provides native ML-based cost anomaly detection for EC2 with configurable alerts?

options.label: A
options.text: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML on historical spend patterns; configure a monitor for EC2 and set a threshold for SNS or email alerts.

options.label: B
options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor Cost Optimization checks continuously monitor spend for anomalies and send automated SNS alerts.

options.label: C
options.text: AWS Budgets with an anomaly-type budget detects cost spikes and alerts when daily spend deviates from expected.

options.label: D
options.text: CloudWatch billing alarms with dynamic thresholds automatically detect anomalous EC2 spending using CloudWatch Anomaly Detection.

distractors.C: Budgets alerts on actual vs. budgeted spend; they do not use ML to detect deviations from historical patterns.
distractors.D: CloudWatch Anomaly Detection applies to CloudWatch metrics; Cost Anomaly Detection is purpose-built for billing anomalies.
distractors.B: Trusted Advisor provides recommendations; it does not have ML-based spend anomaly detection with configurable alerts.

explanation: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection trains ML models on your historical spending patterns. Service-level monitors (e.g., EC2) detect unusual cost increases above configured thresholds and send alerts via SNS or email, enabling rapid investigation of unexpected spend.

stem: Large EC2 instances run batch jobs from 8 PM to 6 AM daily. The rest of the day they are idle. What is the most cost-effective purchasing strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Spot Instances; batch workloads that checkpoint and restart on interruption benefit from up to 90% savings versus On-Demand.

options.label: B
options.text: Purchase Dedicated Hosts; billed per host-hour they provide savings for regular daily workloads.

options.label: C
options.text: Purchase 1-year Reserved Instances; they provide up to 40% savings for the 10-hour daily usage window.

options.label: D
options.text: Use On-Demand with EventBridge stop/start scheduling to eliminate idle charges.

distractors.C: RIs for 10 hours/day (42% utilization) provide limited savings; Spot provides much deeper discounts for interruptible batch workloads.
distractors.D: On-Demand with stop/start eliminates idle costs but still pays full On-Demand rates during the 10-hour run window.
distractors.B: Dedicated Hosts are for compliance/licensing needs; they are significantly more expensive than Spot.

explanation: Spot Instances are the canonical choice for batch processing. Designing jobs with checkpointing to S3/EBS allows recovery from interruptions. The 2-minute interruption notice enables graceful checkpoints. Up to 90% savings versus On-Demand far exceeds RI or other alternatives for this pattern.

stem: Data transfer costs are 25% of the total bill, mostly EC2-to-S3 in the same region. What reduces this cost?

options.label: A
options.text: Move EC2 instances to the same AZ as the S3 bucket; same-AZ transfers are free.

options.label: B
options.text: Compress objects before upload; smaller object size reduces transfer costs proportionally.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration; it routes traffic through CloudFront edge locations with lower transfer rates.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3; EC2-to-S3 traffic through a Gateway Endpoint incurs no data transfer charges within the same region.

distractors.C: Transfer Acceleration accelerates uploads from internet clients and costs more per GB; it does not reduce EC2-to-S3 transfer costs.
distractors.A: S3 is a regional service without AZ affinity; there is no same-AZ discount for EC2-to-S3.
distractors.B: Compression reduces data size and time but the billing is on the compressed bytes transferred; it doesn't eliminate the charge.

explanation: AWS does not charge for EC2-to-S3 data transfer when traffic flows through an S3 Gateway Endpoint. Without an endpoint, traffic uses the internet-facing S3 endpoint and incurs regional data transfer charges. Adding a Gateway Endpoint to the VPC route table eliminates these costs at no additional charge.

stem: The finance team needs monthly reports showing costs broken down by application across EC2, RDS, and ELB resources. Which feature enables this?

options.label: A
options.text: Use CloudWatch to correlate resource utilization with the Cost and Usage Report to estimate per-application costs.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable AWS Resource Groups per application; AWS automatically generates cost reports for each resource group.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a separate AWS account per application; consolidated billing reports per-account spend corresponding to per-application costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Apply cost allocation tags (Application=CRM, Application=ERP, etc.) to all resources, activate them in Billing, and use Cost Explorer to group costs by the Application tag.

distractors.C: Separate accounts per application is a valid isolation strategy but adds management overhead and may not suit shared services.
distractors.A: Correlating utilization with CUR is complex and inaccurate compared to direct cost allocation tagging.
distractors.B: Resource Groups organizes resources; it does not automatically generate cost reports. Cost allocation tags in Billing are the mechanism.

explanation: Cost allocation tags must be applied to resources and activated in the Billing console. Once active, Cost Explorer can group and filter costs by tag value, showing per-application spend across all resource types (EC2, RDS, ELB) for any time period.
